title: Your rights at work
kw: employment rights worker rights minimum wage holidays annual leave sick pay contract payslip breaks hours direitos trabalhistas salário mínimo férias
short: Everyone working legally in Ireland has the same rights, whatever their nationality. The adult minimum wage is €14.15 an hour, and you are entitled to a written contract, payslips, breaks and 4 weeks of paid holidays.
steps: **Contract:** the main terms in writing within 5 days of starting, and the rest within a month.
**Pay:** at least the minimum wage, with a payslip showing gross pay and every deduction.
**Hours:** no more than 48 hours a week on average. A 15-minute break after 4.5 hours of work and 30 minutes after 6 hours, and 11 hours of rest between working days.
**Time off:** 4 weeks of paid annual leave, 10 public holidays, and 5 days of paid sick leave a year (70% of pay, up to €110 a day).

**Family leave:** 26 weeks’ maternity leave, 2 weeks’ paternity leave, 9 weeks’ parent’s leave and 26 weeks’ unpaid parental leave. See [Maternity, Paternity and Parent’s Benefit](#/s/parent-benefits).
**Dismissal:** after 12 months in the job you can bring an unfair dismissal claim.

cases.q: What is the minimum wage if I am under 20?

a: The adult minimum wage is due to rise to €14.94 an hour on 1 January 2027.

cases.q: My employer gives me food or accommodation
a: They can count it towards the minimum wage only at fixed rates: €1.27 an hour for food, and €33.42 a week or €4.77 a day for accommodation.
Discrimination is illegal on nine grounds, including gender, age, disability, race and religion. See [Complain about an employer](#/s/wrc-complaint).

cases.q: I am on an employment permit
a: You have exactly the same statutory rights as an Irish employee.

src: Citizens Information · Employees’ rights and entitlements

title: Complain about an employer (WRC)
kw: wrc workplace relations commission complaint employer unpaid wages unfair dismissal dispute labour court reclamar empregador processo trabalhista
short: If your employer breaks your rights and will not fix it, you complain online to the Workplace Relations Commission. You normally have 6 months from the incident.
steps: Raise the problem with your employer first, in writing if you can.
If it is not resolved, fill in the WRC **online complaint form**.
The WRC sends the complaint to mediation or to an adjudicator, who holds a hearing and gives a decision.
You can appeal an adjudicator’s decision to the Labour Court.

a: The limit can be extended by up to another 6 months if there was a reasonable cause for the delay.

cases.q: I am paid less than the minimum wage
a: On the form you choose either an inspector’s investigation or an adjudicator’s hearing. You cannot use both.

cases.q: I just want to ask a question first
a: Phone WRC Information and Customer Service on (059) 917 8990, Monday to Friday, 9.30am to 1pm and 2pm to 5pm.

title: Start a business
kw: start a business register company sole trader business name cro limited company local enterprise office abrir empresa mei cnpj
short: Pick a structure, register the name or the company with the Companies Registration Office, and register for tax with Revenue. Your Local Enterprise Office gives free advice and can offer grants.
steps: **Choose a structure.** As a sole trader you and the business are one: simple, but you are personally responsible for its debts. A limited company is a separate legal entity. A solicitor or accountant can advise.

**Register the name.** A sole trader who trades under a name that is not their own must register it with the Companies Registration Office (CRO). A company is incorporated with the CRO through its online system, CORE.
**Register for tax** with Revenue. Sole traders pay income tax by self-assessment: see [Tax if you are self-employed](#/s/self-employed-tax). Companies pay corporation tax.
**Get support.** Contact your [Local Enterprise Office](https://www.localenterprise.ie/) for training, mentoring and grants.

cases.q: I am not an Irish or EU citizen
a: Citizens of the EEA, Switzerland and the UK need no permission to set up a business. Others need an immigration permission that allows it, for example through the Start-up Entrepreneur Programme: ask Immigration Service Delivery.

You may keep part of your payment while you start up, through the [Back to Work Enterprise Allowance](https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-social-protection/services/back-to-work-enterprise-allowance/) or the Short-Term Enterprise Allowance.
